![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069995/assets/3b603e45dd1e5fe3073cad13a5577389736c1103840f3f904e29e738b4f2fd2e.png)

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the upper half plane bounded by the polar circles $r=1,$ $r=2,$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to the square of its distance from the origin. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin.
worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=k{r}^{2},$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }k{r}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{{r}^{4}}{4}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta {|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =k\cdot \frac{15}{4}\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{15k\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=k{r}^{2}=\frac{4M{r}^{2}}{15\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta {|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{6}(64-1)\cdot (\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{14M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
